name: Bianca Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate French into English for small wine estates, cheese makers and food exporters, so labels, websites, export forms and sometimes a family history for the back of a bottle. A few times a year I'm a liaison interpreter, which means I walk round a vineyard or a trade fair with a British buyer and the grower and help them talk. I work from the kitchen table in our small house, and Luc, my husband, is an electrician, so he's out early in his van. I use one of the AI tools now and then for export forms, but never for anything with a family's story in it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the vineyard visits, when the grower's grandmother brings out bread and the buyer finally relaxes. I'm still learning wine vocabulary, and the senior translators know far more about soils and grapes than I do. What wears me out is the export paperwork, which is dull and always urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people still want a real person to tell a family's story, and that's reassuring. I'd say it to my growers and at church. I might share a nice post from a winery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. Luc's work is steady, my clients are loyal small businesses, and the dull forms I'd happily let the software do. I use AI for export forms, but never for anything with a family's story in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my clients and offer them a package: website, labels and visits. I'd use the AI tool more for the export forms, maybe saving three hours a week. I'd do a wine course in the evenings, about three hundred, to get my vocabulary up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Luc's work is steady. How much do you rely on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot, honestly. Luc earns more than me, and our mortgage is in both names but he covers most of it. My savings are about three months of my own costs. We're careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More visits, more time with the growers. And maybe start thinking about children, which we've talked about for next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small producers still need a person who knows them, and that big firms using AI isn't the whole story. I'd say it calmly to clients. I'd encourage people to support local businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think labels and websites go to AI within two years. My growers are careful with money and they'd try it. I'd keep the visits and some stories, but maybe half my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the interpreting visits harder and pitch myself to an export agency as a person who handles relationships. I'd learn the AI tools properly, since others have now. We'd probably hold off on children a year until I see where my income lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not afraid for the house, because of Luc, but afraid for my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Holding off on children. How does Luc feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luc says we can manage on his pay. But I want to bring something in too, so I'd want a year to sort my work out. We'd pray about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your growers would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's an old couple who make goat's cheese and don't use computers at all. If the buyers expect everything online in English, they'd struggle more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities need to stick together. I'd say government shouldn't just pay people to sit at home. I'd say it quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, my translation work is gone by 2028. Even the stories would be done by AI. The only thing left is being there in person, at the vineyards, until robots in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask one of my wine estates for a job in their tasting room or cellar, which is hands-on and in person. I'd stop translating once it dried up. We'd lean on Luc's pay, though his work could change by 2031 too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. For both of us, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Luc's work could change. Does that worry you more than yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because he's our main income. An electrician gets three years more than a translator, but then what? I try not to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents we're fine for now. And that we'd need their help if things got bad. They have a small garden and chickens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan properly. I'd say small businesses should band together. I'd suggest it to my growers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is fair for me. I'd translate for two or three years, then move into the cellar work. I'd hope to be useful in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the wine course and a cellar hand certificate, about five hundred. I'd keep translating and save more, about two hundred a month. We'd try for a child in year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said bands together. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A group of growers could share one person who handles export and visits, and that person could be me. It's a cooperative idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the child come before the job change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably around the same time. Luc wants children soon. I'd want both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to adjust as families. I'd say it at church. I'd be fairly peaceful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably translate for five or six years. Then move into cellar or vineyard work. I'd be in my late thirties, with children, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and slowly learn the cellar work. We'd start a family soon. I'd wait to see how the industry changes before jumping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. Mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most if translation ended?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing the family stories for the bottles. I'd miss that a lot. But I'd still hear them, at the vineyard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach your children French?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course. I'd teach my children French, maybe not for a job, but for their grandparents and the growers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Luc's work is also at risk soon after. What would help is apprenticeships in wine and food that welcome people my age. Support for small producers too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much I love the visits. Being there in person is the part of my job I'd keep forever.

headlineQuote: Being there in person is the part of my job I'd keep forever.
portrait: A **27-year-old** French–English translator for wine estates and food makers, married to Luc, an electrician.
Uses **AI for forms** but never for family stories.
Feels **calm** in AI Plateau, anxious as labels move to AI.
Plans a move into **cellar work** and thinks about a growers' cooperative role.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, since Luc's work is at risk soon after.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** in wine and food for people her age.
